# Students per teacher

**Cambridge has fewer students per teacher than the four nearby districts it is compared with here.** In 2024–25, Cambridge had about 8.7 students per teacher — the lowest ratio of the five, and below the statewide figure of about 10.9. This measure — **K-12 students per teacher** — is a district-wide staffing ratio: the total K-12 enrollment divided by the number of teachers. It is not NYSED's official class size (which counts only specific classrooms), but it is a fair way to compare districts and track change over time.

The chart below shows how students per teacher has changed since teacher counts became available (2017–18 onward). It stops at 2024–25: NYSED has published 2025–26 enrollment but not yet the 2025–26 teacher counts.

```{python}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
import os
import sys

sys.path.insert(0, os.getcwd())

import polars as pl
from plotnine import (
    aes,
    geom_line,
    geom_point,
    ggplot,
    labs,
    scale_color_manual,
    scale_x_continuous,
    scale_y_continuous,
)
from great_tables import GT, loc, md, style

import comparisons as cc

# Years shown. Teacher counts start in 2017-18. NYSED had not posted the
# 2025-26 staff file when this chapter was last updated, so the chapter stops
# at 2024-25 even though 2025-26 enrollment is in the panel.
FIRST_YEAR, LAST_YEAR = 2018, 2025
SPAN = f"{cc.school_year_label(FIRST_YEAR)} to {cc.school_year_label(LAST_YEAR)}"

spt = (
    cc.panel_for(cc.GRAPH_GROUP, since=FIRST_YEAR)
    .filter(pl.col("year_end") <= LAST_YEAR)
    .select(
        "district", "region", "year_end",
        "k12_enrollment", "num_teachers", "k12_students_per_teacher",
    )
    .drop_nulls("k12_students_per_teacher")
)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Checks on the statements made in the text of this chapter. If the data
# change so that a statement is no longer true, the page fails to build
# instead of quietly showing text that disagrees with its own charts.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
def _val(district, year_end, col="k12_students_per_teacher"):
    return spt.filter(
        (pl.col("district") == district) & (pl.col("year_end") == year_end)
    )[col].item()


def _ratios(year_end):
    rows = spt.filter(pl.col("year_end") == year_end)
    return dict(zip(rows["district"], rows["k12_students_per_teacher"]))


first, last = _ratios(FIRST_YEAR), _ratios(LAST_YEAR)
change = {d: last[d] - first[d] for d in last}

# Cambridge's own numbers.
assert _val(cc.FOCUS, FIRST_YEAR, "k12_enrollment") == 869
assert _val(cc.FOCUS, LAST_YEAR, "k12_enrollment") == 741
assert _val(cc.FOCUS, FIRST_YEAR, "num_teachers") == 85
assert _val(cc.FOCUS, LAST_YEAR, "num_teachers") == 85
assert round(first[cc.FOCUS], 1) == 10.2 and round(last[cc.FOCUS], 1) == 8.7
assert round(change[cc.FOCUS], 1) == -1.5
_cam_teachers = spt.filter(pl.col("district") == cc.FOCUS)["num_teachers"]
assert (_cam_teachers.min(), _cam_teachers.max()) == (77, 94)

# Cambridge among the five: lowest in the last year; only Salem lower in the
# first year. Cambridge and Salem traded places: Cambridge was the lower of
# the two in 2018-19, 2020-21, 2023-24 and 2024-25.
assert min(last, key=last.get) == cc.FOCUS
assert [d for d in first if first[d] < first[cc.FOCUS]] == ["Salem"]
assert [
    _yr for _yr in range(FIRST_YEAR, LAST_YEAR + 1)
    if _ratios(_yr)[cc.FOCUS] < _ratios(_yr)["Salem"]
] == [2019, 2021, 2024, 2025]

# Changes in the other four: all fell; Schuylerville and Greenwich fell most.
assert all(v < 0 for v in change.values())
assert round(change["Schuylerville"], 1) == -2.0
assert round(change["Greenwich"], 1) == -1.9
assert round(change["Salem"], 1) == -0.2
assert round(change["Hoosick Falls"], 1) == -0.3
assert round(first["Salem"], 1) == 9.4 and round(last["Salem"], 1) == 9.2

# Cambridge among all twelve Washington County-area districts in the last year.
_twelve = (
    cc.panel_for(cc.TABLE_GROUP, since=LAST_YEAR)
    .filter(pl.col("year_end") == LAST_YEAR)
    .sort("k12_students_per_teacher")
)
assert _twelve["district"].to_list()[:4] == [
    "Fort Edward", "Hartford", "Whitehall", cc.FOCUS,
]

# Statewide: all districts' K-12 students divided by all districts' teachers.
def _statewide(year_end):
    rows = cc.load_panel().filter(
        (pl.col("year_end") == year_end)
        & pl.col("k12_enrollment").is_not_null()
        & (pl.col("num_teachers") > 0)
    )
    return rows["k12_enrollment"].sum(), rows["num_teachers"].sum()


(_e0, _t0), (_e1, _t1) = _statewide(FIRST_YEAR), _statewide(LAST_YEAR)
assert round(_e0 / _t0, 1) == 12.7 and round(_e1 / _t1, 1) == 10.9
assert round(100 * (_e1 / _e0 - 1)) == -10  # statewide K-12 enrollment
assert round(100 * (_t1 / _t0 - 1)) == 5    # statewide teachers
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-students-per-teacher
#| fig-cap: "K–12 students per teacher by school year ending, 2018 (2017–18) through 2025 (2024–25). Lower means fewer students per teacher. Source: NYSED Enrollment database (K-12 enrollment) and Student & Educator database (teacher counts)."
g = spt
cambridge = g.filter(pl.col("district") == cc.FOCUS)

(
    ggplot(g, aes("year_end", "k12_students_per_teacher", color="district"))
    + geom_line(size=1)
    + geom_point(size=1.8)
    + geom_line(cambridge, size=2.4)  # emphasize the focus district
    + scale_color_manual(
        values=cc.PALETTE, name="", limits=cc.district_order(cc.GRAPH_GROUP)
    )
    + scale_x_continuous(breaks=list(range(FIRST_YEAR, LAST_YEAR + 1)))
    + labs(
        x="School year ending",
        y="K–12 students per teacher",
        title=f"Students per teacher, {SPAN}",
    )
    + cc.theme_ccs()
)
```

Cambridge's ratio has fallen over time because **enrollment dropped while the number of teachers ended where it started**. In 2017–18, Cambridge had 869 students and 85 teachers (10.2 students per teacher). By 2024–25, enrollment had fallen to 741 (see the [Enrollment](enrollment.qmd) chapter) and the district again had 85 teachers — pushing the ratio down to 8.7. In between, the teacher count ranged from 77 to 94. Counts of people move around from year to year in small districts, so single-year swings in the chart should not be read closely. [CLAUDE: Cambridge's count went 82, 94, 85 in the last three years. I have not found the reason for the 94. The count is people, not full-time equivalents, so a change in part-time staffing moves the ratio without changing teaching time. Worth asking the district what happened in 2023–24.]

Only Salem had a lower ratio in 2017–18. The two districts traded places several times after that; Cambridge has been the lower of the two in 2023–24 and 2024–25, and now has the lowest ratio of the five. Among all twelve Washington County-area districts, three smaller districts had lower ratios in 2024–25: Fort Edward, Hartford, and Whitehall.

Falling ratios are not unique to Cambridge. Statewide, K-12 students per teacher fell from about 12.7 to about 10.9 over the same years, as enrollment declined about 10% and the number of teachers rose about 5%.

## What this measure is (and isn't)

**Students per teacher is a staffing ratio, not a class-size count.** It divides K-12 enrollment by the number of teachers in the district, which includes:

- All teachers, not just those leading regular classes (so art, music, special education, and other specialists are counted)
- Teacher **headcount** (the number of people employed), not full-time-equivalents (so part-time teachers count as one each)
- All grades K-12, not just the grades NYSED reports for class size

This makes it an **approximate measure** for comparing districts and tracking change — useful for the big picture, but not the same as the number of children in a typical classroom. NYSED's official class-size figures cover only a handful of specific grades and subjects, and they exist only since 2018–19. For a deeper dive into those measures, see the [Class size and students per teacher: all measures](../exploratory/class-size-all-measures.qmd) appendix.

## What it means for Cambridge

Cambridge's low students-per-teacher ratio reflects a choice: **maintain small classes and preserve programs even as enrollment falls.** That choice has implications: [CLAUDE: The data show that the ratio fell. They do not show why, and they say nothing about class size. The statewide ratio fell more than Cambridge's (1.8 against 1.5), so much of this is a general pattern. If the board has said this was its aim, cite where. Otherwise I would describe what happened and drop "a choice" and "small classes".]

- **Higher spending per pupil.** Fewer students to spread fixed costs (salaries, benefits, facilities) across means spending per student runs higher (see the [Spending](spending.qmd) chapter).
- **Budget pressure.** The same tax base must support more teachers per student than neighboring districts, which can strain the budget when state aid doesn't keep pace. [CLAUDE: State aid pays a large share of the budget, and the tax base has grown 61% since 2014–15. I would say only that more teachers per student costs more per student.]
- **Classroom experience.** Fewer students per teacher means more individual attention, which is a strength Cambridge has maintained even as enrollment declined. [CLAUDE: "A strength" is a judgment, and the site is meant to inform and not recommend. The ratio counts every teacher, including specialists and part-timers, so it does not tell us how much attention a child gets in a typical classroom. I would cut this bullet or restate it as a fact.]

The table below shows where each district stood in 2017–18 and 2024–25, and how much their staffing ratios changed.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-students-per-teacher-change
#| tbl-cap: "K–12 students per teacher in 2017–18 and 2024–25, with change, by district."
g = spt.filter(pl.col("year_end").is_in([FIRST_YEAR, LAST_YEAR]))
y0, y1 = str(FIRST_YEAR), str(LAST_YEAR)

wide = (
    g.with_columns(
        pl.when(pl.col("region") == "Washington County").then(0).otherwise(1).alias("_rank")
    )
    .pivot(values="k12_students_per_teacher", index=["_rank", "region", "district"], on="year_end")
    .sort(["_rank", "district"])
    .drop("_rank")
)

wide = wide.with_columns((pl.col(y1) - pl.col(y0)).alias("change"))

(
    GT(wide, rowname_col="district", groupname_col="region")
    .tab_header(
        title="Students per teacher change",
        subtitle=(
            f"School-year-ending {y0} ({cc.school_year_label(FIRST_YEAR)}) and "
            f"{y1} ({cc.school_year_label(LAST_YEAR)}), with change"
        ),
    )
    .fmt_number(columns=[y0, y1, "change"], decimals=1)
    .tab_spanner(label="School year ending", columns=[y0, y1])
    .cols_label(change=md(f"Change<br>{y0}→{y1}"))
    .tab_style(
        style=[style.fill(color="#FCEFB4"), style.text(weight="bold")],
        locations=[
            loc.body(rows=pl.col("district") == cc.FOCUS),
            loc.stub(rows=pl.col("district") == cc.FOCUS),
        ],
    )
    .tab_source_note(
        md(
            "**Source:** NYSED Enrollment database (K-12 enrollment) and "
            "Student &amp; Educator database (teacher counts). Ratio = district "
            "K-12 enrollment ÷ teacher headcount; an approximate comparison "
            "measure, not official class size. Year = school-year-ending "
            "(2025 = 2024–25)."
        )
    )
)
```

**Cambridge's ratio fell by 1.5 students per teacher** (from 10.2 to 8.7). Schuylerville and Greenwich saw larger drops (2.0 and 1.9 respectively) but started from higher levels. The ratio fell in all five districts; the smallest changes were in Salem (from 9.4 to 9.2) and Hoosick Falls (down 0.3).
